title: Naomi and Ruth Return to Bethlehem

date.label: Undated Ruth narrative
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Ruth 1:1 opens "in the days when the judges judged," anchoring the story in the Judges era; it names no judge, king, or year and yields no absolute date.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre, live 2026-11-23.

claims.claim: A famine in the land drives Elimelech, an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah, to sojourn with his family in the fields of Moab. The text states no cause for the famine.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: Elimelech's family are "Ephrathites of Beth-lehem in Judah" (JPS 1917).
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: Bethlehem lies about 8 km south of Jerusalem on the central watershed ridge, on the Jerusalem–Hebron road, at a crossroad of wadis to the Dead Sea and the coastal plain, with six springs in its surroundings.

"Ephrathah" may have been the name of the town itself or of the clan and district around it; "Ephrathite" marked belonging to the old-established families of Bethlehem. The evidence does not settle which.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Ephrathah," read in full.

claims.claim: The identification "Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem" is a gloss; Ephrath is an unknown locality, and the traditional Rachel's-tomb site rests on a confusion of Ephrath with the clan-name Ephrathah.
claims.evidence: Reuse: `clm-ij-063` (debated), Skinner pp. 434–439 read in full (per reuse file).

claims.claim: Bethlehem was occupied from the Middle Bronze Age into the Iron Age, with continuity into Iron IIA–B; the Khalet al-Jam'a necropolis (at least 100 shaft tombs, c. 2200–650 BC) served a settlement of some substance in the area.
claims.evidence: Nigro 2015, §§4–5.2, pp. 10–16; Nigro et al. 2018 read in full (see R01-S02).

claims.claim: The precise location of the Iron Age town of Bethlehem before the 7th century BC is not proved; the Basilica-hill location is plausible only for Iron IIC–III (701–535 BC), and no Iron Age I settlement structure has been excavated.

A 7th-century BC fiscal bulla reading "in the seventh / Bethlehem / [for the] king" is the first extra-biblical attestation of the name Bethlehem; it proves Bethlehem was a city in the Kingdom of Judah in the late 8th–7th centuries BC, and nothing about the Judges era.
claims.evidence: IAA announcement 2012, via BiblePlaces, read in full; Nigro 2015, §5.4.

claims.claim: A proposed Amarna-letter mention of Bethlehem ("Beth Lahmi," EA 290) was rejected by scholars; it does not attest the town in the 14th century BC.
Elimelech dies in Moab; his sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth; after about ten years Mahlon and Chilion also die, leaving Naomi widowed and childless.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: A widow in ancient Israel, especially one without grown sons, often lost income, legal protection, and a place in the family inheritance, and was among the most vulnerable members of society; her security depended on children, her own family, or her late husband's relatives.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Widow," read in full.

claims.claim: Naomi returns because she heard in Moab that the LORD had "visited His people in giving them bread" — the narrative's stated reason for the return.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: Naomi's farewell blessing asks God to show *hesed* to Orpah and Ruth as they showed *hesed* to the dead and to her, and to grant each *menuchah* (rest) in a new husband's house; the two blessings frame the women's past loyalty as the basis of the prayer.
claims.evidence: Abin 2021, pp. 74–77, read in part; Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full.

claims.claim: *Menuchah* / *manoach* ("rest") in Ruth concretely means security and basic stability, associated in Israel with God's promises and the promised land; Naomi seeks it for Ruth first in 1:9 and again in 3:1.
claims.evidence: Potgieter & Taute 2020, read in part; Abin 2021.

claims.claim: "Ruth cleaved unto her" — the verb *davaq* (clinging, adhering) marks Ruth's decision against Orpah's turning back.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: Ruth's speech is a formal binding oath: paired pledges (go/lodge, people/God, die/be buried) sealed by the self-imprecatory formula "the LORD do so to me, and more also, if aught but death part thee and me." The same formula occurs twelve times in the Old Testament (Ruth once; Samuel and Kings eleven times).
claims.evidence: Meridian Magazine account, read in full (Campbell read in part — see R01-S10/S11); Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full.

claims.claim: Campbell reads the oath's vague penalty as gestured rather than spoken — a symbolic throat-cutting gesture, probably echoing animal slaughter in covenant ratification (Gen 15:7–17; Jer 34:18–20).
claims.evidence: Campbell 1975, Ruth 1:16–17 notes read directly in part (pp. 74–75, via archive.org); Meridian Magazine account corroborates.

claims.claim: Naomi asks to be called Mara ("bitter") because the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with her: she went out full and the LORD brought her back empty. This is her judgement on her circumstances, not a permanent name change — the text calls her Naomi again thereafter.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre; Potgieter & Taute 2020, read in part.

claims.claim: "Ruth the Moabitess" is the narrator's repeated designation for Ruth: verified in 1:22 and in 2:2, 2:6, 2:21 (read live); the proposal also records it at 4:5 and 4:10 (not re-verified in this dossier).
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917, chs. 1–2 read in full live; ch. 4 occurrences per proposal §5 / read record.

claims.claim: Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem "in the beginning of barley harvest" — the first grain harvest of the year, in early spring around Passover; in the hill country the barley harvest ran into May, several weeks before wheat.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Barley Harvest," read in full; Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full.

claims.claim: Severe, prolonged drought is attested in the southern Levant around 1250–1100 BCE by high-resolution Sea of Galilee pollen cores; this is regional climate context only and does not date or explain Ruth's famine.
claims.evidence: Langgut, Finkelstein & Litt 2013, full text read live 2026-11-23 (see R01-S09); the Late Bronze dry event is "the most pronounced dry episode during the Bronze and Iron Ages," with the lowest arboreal pollen values in the sequence at ~1250–1100 BCE (pp. 160–161).

claims.claim: The route between Bethlehem and Moab is not stated in the text; three routes are proposed (northern via Jericho, ~76 miles; central via En Gedi and the Lisan, ~62 miles; southern around the Dead Sea, ~102 miles). None is established.
claims.evidence: Crossroads Bible Church (Udd) 2026, read in full (popular geography summary, not peer-reviewed).

claims.claim: The tension between Ruth the Moabitess being taken as wife and the Deut 23 exclusion of the Moabite "for ever" is noted, not resolved; no editorial line is taken in this dossier.
claims.evidence: Reuse: `conn-deu-06-023` (thematic, probable); `clm-deu-06-043/045` (established).

connections.note: Another Bethlehem in Judah notice from the Judges era: a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah is hired by Micah. The same town name in the same period frames Ruth's home town.
A Levite's concubine comes from her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah, and the two travel from Bethlehem toward Gibeah. Bethlehem appears here as a settled Judahite town on a travelled road.

Rachel dies and is buried on the way to Ephrath, glossed in the text as Bethlehem. The identification of Ephrath with Bethlehem is debated among scholars, so the link is given as the text presents it, not as settled geography.
The origin of Moab in the story of Lot and his daughters. Ruth's Moabite identity reaches back to this account, which the narrative itself presents as the background of Israel's neighbour.

The Ammonite and the Moabite are excluded from the congregation for ever, for inhospitality on the march and for hiring Balaam. Ruth, a Moabitess, enters Bethlehem and the story of Israel; the tension with this law is noted here and left open.
Israel is told not to distress Moab, for Ar was given to the children of Lot. The passage sets the geographical and kinship background of the land Elimelech's family enters.
David's father Jesse is called an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah — the same designation Ruth 1:2 gives Elimelech's family, tying the two households to the same old Bethlehem families.

"But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel." The prophet joins the two names Ruth also joins, and looks for a ruler from this small town.
The first sheaf of the harvest is to be waved before the Lord before the new crop is eaten. Ruth's return at the beginning of barley harvest falls at the opening of this festal season.

The forgotten sheaf, the beaten olive tree, and the gleaned vineyard are left for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem as widow and foreigner, the very people this law provides for.
"Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child." The law states God's protection of widows; Naomi and Ruth embody the vulnerability it addresses.

"There was a famine in the land: and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there." Famine driving a household to sojourn in a foreign land is an established pattern in the patriarchal stories, and Ruth 1 follows it.
Seven descendants of Saul are put to death "in the beginning of barley harvest," the same seasonal marker that closes Ruth 1, showing the phrase as a recognized time stamp in the historical books.

RCL-01-020 carried as established: the second reader independently confirmed "Ruth the Moabitess" at Ruth 4:5 and 4:10 on Mechon Mamre by live fetch, closing the dossier's re-verification gap (the dossier capped it at probable only because the occurrences were not re-verified there).
